what_its_for: Indomethacin is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to relieve pain, swelling, and stiffness caused by conditions such as arthritis, gout, bursitis, and tendinitis. It works by reducing the chemicals in your body that cause pain and inflammation.
how_to_take: Take indomethacin exactly as your doctor prescribes. Always take it with food, milk, or an antacid to help protect your stomach. Swallow capsules whole — do not crush, chew, or open them. If you are taking the extended-release (SR) capsule, swallow it whole without breaking it. If you are using the suppository form, follow the instructions provided and wash your hands before and after use.
dosing: Your dose will depend on your condition and what your doctor recommends. A common starting dose for adults is 25 mg taken 2 to 3 times per day. Your doctor may increase this to 50 mg three times per day if needed. Do not take more than 200 mg per day unless your doctor tells you to. For extended-release capsules, the usual dose is 75 mg once or twice daily. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store indomethacin at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it past the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking indomethacin, as it increases the risk of stomach bleeding. Do not take aspirin or other NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen or naproxen) unless your doctor tells you it is safe. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medication affects you, since it can cause dizziness or blurred vision. Limit prolonged sun exposure, as this medicine may make your skin more sensitive to sunlight. Do not take indomethacin right before or after heart bypass surgery (CABG).
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice: black, tarry, or bloody stools; vomit that looks like coffee grounds; severe stomach pain; chest pain or shortness of breath; sudden weakness or trouble speaking (signs of stroke); swelling of your face, lips, or throat; skin rash, blisters, or peeling; yellowing of your skin or eyes; significant weight gain or swelling in your legs or feet; decreased urination; or unusual bruising or bleeding. Also contact your doctor if your pain or inflammation does not improve.
when_it_works: Indomethacin usually starts to reduce pain and inflammation within 30 minutes to a few hours after your first dose. For conditions like arthritis, the full benefit may take 1 to 2 weeks of regular use. For acute gout, many patients feel significant relief within 24 to 48 hours.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over): Use with extra caution, as you are at higher risk for stomach bleeding, kidney problems, and heart side effects. Your doctor may prescribe a lower dose. Pregnancy: Do NOT use indomethacin after 20 weeks of pregnancy unless specifically directed by your doctor, as it can harm the unborn baby's kidneys and heart. Avoid it especially in the third trimester. Breastfeeding: Small amounts may pass into breast milk; talk to your doctor before using. Children: Indomethacin is generally not recommended for children under 14 years old except in specific situations (such as in premature newborns for a heart condition), and only under close medical supervision. Kidney or liver disease: Use with caution; your doctor may need to monitor you closely or adjust your dose.
